question: The Commission has approved Belgium’s law to ban disposable vapes, and many Member States, including Ireland, are moving in the same direction. Although more independent research is needed into the health impacts of vaping, current research points to potentially severe physical and psychological implications, especially for children.
We already know that disposable vapes are harming the environment through pollution with toxic chemicals and microplastics.

I have called for a nation-wide ban on disposable vapes in Ireland, and believe that a harmonised EU-wide ban on disposable vapes is urgently necessary to ensure the proper functioning of the single market, as well as to prevent further damage to public health and the environment, as long as the effects of vaping remain unknown. 1.

When will the Commission conduct an independent, scientific impact assessment on the implications of vapes for young people, overall health and the environment, preventing, to the maximum extent, industry influence?

Will the Commission come forward with a proposal to revise the Tobacco Products Directive1in order to ban the sale of disposable vapes and regulate the marketing of e-cigarettes towards children across the single market?

Directive 2014/40/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 3 April 2014 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States concerning the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco and related products and repealing Directive 2001/37/EC (OJ L 127, 29.4.2014, p. 1).
answer: There are no safe levels of tobacco consumption, including from smoke-free nicotine products. In addition, given the novelty of some nicotine products and the evolving evidence especially on medium- and long-term health effects, scientific evidence needs to be carefully considered.

Following a request from the Commission, the Scientific Committee on Health, Environmental and Emerging Risks underlined the negative health effects associated with e-cigarettes and concluded there is moderate evidence that they may be a gateway to smoking for young people (2). Also, whereas they can be used to halt tobacco consumption, e-cigarette users sometimes become ‘dual users’.

In the EU, advertising and promotion of e-cigarettes and refill containers are prohibited in Information Society Services, printed publications, the radio, audiovisual media and in contribution to radio programmes, events, and activities (3).

While Member States are responsible for regulating age limits and sales arrangements for tobacco and related products, they are encouraged to prevent their sales to children and adolescents (4). The Commission is conducting an evaluation of the EU legislative framework on tobacco control (5). It encompasses the Tobacco Products Directive (6), the Tobacco Advertising Directive (7), and other tobacco control policies.

The way forward will be contingent upon the findings of this evaluation. The Commission is also committed to fully implement Article 5.3. of the framework Convention on Tobacco Control (8) which requires that ‘in setting and implementing their public health policies with respect to tobacco control, Parties shall act to protect these policies from commercial and other vested interests of the tobacco industry’ (9).
